content: Community health workers (CHWs) are individuals who provide healthcare support within their own communities. They are chosen by the community, are accountable to the community for their activities, and are supported by the health system, though they are not necessarily part of its formal structure. Their training is shorter compared to professional healthcare workers. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This definition, established in the preamble to the Constitution of the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1946 and effective from April 7, 1948, has remained unchanged since its adoption. Health system strengthening involves identifying and implementing changes in a country’s health policies and practices to better address health challenges. This includes initiatives and strategies that enhance one or more functions of the health system, leading to improved health outcomes through better access, coverage, quality, or efficiency. Hospice care refers to organizations or institutions dedicated exclusively to providing palliative care for patients nearing the end of life, either as inpatients or outpatients. Integrated health services are designed to ensure that individuals receive a continuum of care, including health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, disease management, rehabilitation, and palliative care. These services are delivered across various levels and sites of care within the health system, tailored to the needs of individuals throughout their life course. Intersectoral action involves the collaboration of multiple sectors, beyond just health, in designing and implementing public policies aimed at improving healthcare and overall quality of life. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are medical conditions that are not infectious or transmissible between individuals. Examples include heart disease, stroke, cancer, diabetes, and chronic lung diseases. A non-governmental organization (NGO) is an independent entity that operates without direct representation or control by a government or state. People-centered health services are designed to incorporate the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities. These services are based on the principle that individuals, families, and communities are active participants in, as well as beneficiaries of, trusted health systems that address their needs and preferences in a humane and holistic manner. People-centered care emphasizes education and support to enable individuals to make informed decisions and actively participate in their own care. It prioritizes health needs and expectations over a disease-centered approach. Primary health care (PHC) refers to essential healthcare services that are practical, scientifically sound, and socially acceptable. PHC is the cornerstone of a country’s health system, critical for the social and economic development of communities, and serves as the first point of contact with the national health system. It aims to bring healthcare as close as possible to where people live and work, ensuring universal accessibility and affordability for individuals and families at all stages of development. Serious health-related suffering (SHS) occurs when suffering associated with illness or injury cannot be alleviated without medical intervention and significantly compromises physical, social, or emotional functioning. Palliative care focuses on relieving SHS, particularly in cases of life-limiting or life-threatening conditions or at the end of life. Social determinants of health refer to the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age. These circumstances are influenced by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels. They are the primary drivers of health inequities, which are the unfair and avoidable differences in health status observed within and between countries. Universal health coverage (UHC) ensures that individuals receive the health services they need while being protected from financial hardship associated with obtaining care. Health services under UHC encompass health promotion initiatives (e.g., anti-tobacco policies, emergency preparedness), disease prevention activities (e.g., vaccination), and the provision of treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care (e.g., symptom relief, end-of-life care) of sufficient quality to be effective.
